summary:
The Komi Republic stands under the national framework of Russia, which applies in full. The sources record no variation in how these laws operate at the level of the republic, and the jurisdiction is assessed at the national score. A trans visitor to Syktyvkar or anywhere else in the Komi Republic faces the same legal position as a trans visitor elsewhere in the country.

Legal gender recognition and gender-affirming care were banned outright in 2023, when the law prohibiting gender reassignment surgery and legal gender changes on official documents was signed. The Supreme Court has designated the "international LGBT movement" an extremist organisation, and the expanded propaganda law criminalises any public expression, explicitly including anything "justifying" gender transition. Same-sex marriage is banned, gender-marker changes on documents are prohibited, and trans-specific healthcare was effectively banned in the same year.

Penalties are severe and reach foreigners directly. Anyone who violates these laws faces arrest, up to 15 days' detention, and deportation. The 2013 propaganda law is punishable by administrative fines or detention of up to 15 days, escalating to up to four years' imprisonment on a repeat offence. Since the 2023 extremist designation, participation in the designated movement carries two to six years' imprisonment and organising it carries six to ten years.

Enforcement is active and documented. Human Rights Watch recorded 101 extremism-related convictions, about 98 administrative and 3 criminal, for alleged participation in the designated movement or displaying its symbols as of 30 June 2025. Between January 2024 and June 2025 at least 20 people faced criminal charges, including three publishing-house staff charged under article 282.2 who face up to 12 years' imprisonment, while 81 people were convicted in 98 administrative cases under article 20.3 for displaying banned symbols.

The speed and physical character of enforcement are documented. Within 48 hours of the Supreme Court ruling, masked police raided LGBTQ-friendly bars in Moscow, where about 100 patrons at one venue were ordered to face walls, searched and photographed, and at least two other venues were raided the same night. BBC Russian reported on 27 July 2024 on a transgender woman lured by relatives in summer 2021 to a conversion-therapy centre near Novosibirsk, where she was held for nine months and forced to take testosterone, pray and perform manual labour before escaping. In December 2024 the Associated Press reported that a Russian man detained on extremism-related charges over an LGBTQ+ travel agency was found dead in a pretrial detention facility.

Travel advisories reflect these risks. The US State Department advises against all travel to Russia for all travellers regardless of personal characteristic, at Level 4, Do Not Travel, citing wrongful detention risk, the war, and arbitrary law enforcement, and carries warnings directed at LGBT travellers. Official national government warnings explicitly tell LGBT travellers that violations can lead to arrest, detention and deportation. The UK Home Office country policy and information note on sexual orientation and gender identity and expression (v2.0, June 2025) affirms that LGBT+ people in Russia, including the autonomous republic of Chechnya, constitute a particular social group under the refugee convention.
tangentialFactors:
Same-sex sexual activity as such is not criminalised in Russia. The exposure a trans visitor runs is created by expression, symbols and association rather than by private conduct, which is why the propaganda and extremist-designation statutes carry the operative risk.

The principal travel advisories are not framed around personal characteristic at all. The US State Department's Level 4 advisory advises against all travel for every traveller, citing wrongful detention risk, the war, and arbitrary law enforcement, so a trans visitor inherits those general hazards alongside the LGBT-specific warnings the same advisory carries.

Enforcement volume has grown sharply. Meduza reported on 19 June 2025 that cases under Russia's propaganda laws have grown eighteenfold over the past decade, and that fines under those statutes brought more than 60 million rubles ($765,300) into the state budget in the two years preceding.

The Moscow Times reported on 23 June 2025 that arrests, club raids and extremism charges defined LGBTQ+ life in Russia through 2025, and quoted a St Petersburg queer woman describing herself as "a second-class citizen" after the extremist designation.

The UK Home Office note sets the assessment standard for UK asylum claims, holding that LGBT+ people in Russia, including the autonomous republic of Chechnya, constitute a particular social group under the refugee convention. Human Rights Watch has called on governments to offer safe haven to those fleeing Russia.
localsOnly:
The UK Home Office note records at least 139 people in Russia impacted by anti-LGBT+ laws between 2022 and 2024, and assesses that openly LGBT+ people face societal discrimination that may amount to persecution, with the state able but unwilling to protect them.

Of the 101 extremism-related convictions documented by Human Rights Watch as of 30 June 2025, about 98 were administrative and 3 criminal. Eighty-one people were convicted in 98 administrative cases under article 20.3 for displaying banned symbols, while at least 20 people faced criminal charges between January 2024 and June 2025, including three publishing-house staff charged under article 282.2 who face up to 12 years' imprisonment.

Fines under the propaganda statutes generated more than 60 million rubles ($765,300) for the state budget across the two years preceding June 2025.

Residents live under the same 2023 prohibitions as visitors: gender transition is banned, gender-marker changes on official documents are prohibited, same-sex marriage is banned, and trans-specific healthcare was effectively banned in 2023.
outOfScopeNotes:
No source in the inventory reports enforcement, detention conditions, police conduct or court outcomes specific to the Komi Republic. The republic's position is derived from national law and national enforcement data; whether local practice diverges in either direction is unresolved.

The inventory contains no information on organisations, shelters, safe accommodation or care access operating within the Komi Republic, and no sourced statement on whether any gender-affirming care remains obtainable privately anywhere in the country after the 2023 ban.

Entry and border practice for trans passport holders, including document screening at airports serving the republic and the risk of secondary inspection or outing at the border, is not sourced. Document rules are stated at national level only.

Figures attributed to Meduza (19 June 2025) and The Moscow Times (23 June 2025) are as reported by those outlets and are not independently corroborated in the inventory. The UK Home Office note is cited at version 2.0, June 2025, with a page update recorded on 12 August 2026.
